newsitem.title: USA: Delta says 'open skies' pact would not open skies.
newsitem.headline: Delta says 'open skies' pact would not open skies.

text.p: Delta Air Lines Inc. said on Tuesday that any U.S. "open skies" aviation accord with Britain had to assure that new American carriers could compete with the two that now dominate the market between London's Heathrow airport and the United States.

But Delta senior vice president Scott Yohe said the two big carriers, American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp., and British Airways Plc, have made it clear they will not cede any significant number of their Heathrow slots.

The United States and Britain resume talks on a new agreement in London this week, with the aim of forging an accord that would allow airlines of each country unlimited access to cities in the other country.
U.S. officials have said such an accord would be a prerequisite for granting antitrust immunity for a transatlantic marketing alliance planned by American and BA.

Yohe said in a statement and telephone news conference that any agreement would have to include language for the transfer of landing slots from BA to U.S. carriers to ensure full free market open skies competition.
He challenged an AA-commissioned survey issued November 12 that showed the BA alliance would spur airline competition.
Yohe said a Delta-commissioned survey found that "the competition American projects is a fantasy that evaporates when exposed to serious analysis."

The alliance is being opposed by other U.S. airlines and Britain's Virgin Atlantic on grounds it would create a transatlantic monopoly, with the two having 42 percent of the landing slots at Heathrow.
Yohe questioned the AA argument that other slots would be put up for sale to U.S. carriers to fly to Heathrow, saying there would be little interest in selling the valuable slots.
"The market for slots would be overrun by buyers, but there would be almost no sellers," he said.
Yohe said there was also a shortage of parking gate and terminal space. "Right now, space isn't available and open skies won't change that," he said.
Yohe told reporters he understood that U.S. officials were to brief airlines on franchising to allow British carriers to franchise U.S. carriers to feed their transatlantic routes.
But he said he did not know if such a proposal would be taken up in the U.S.-British negotiations.
